analysis.one_liner: Replaces Medicare's private drug plans with a government-run benefit and lets drugs be imported from other countries.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees from February 2006 until the Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have thrown out the Medicare prescription drug program created in 2003, which runs through private insurance companies, and replaced it with a simpler benefit run directly by Medicare. It would have let Medicare negotiate drug prices, required drug makers to sell to Medicare patients at their lowest price anywhere in the world, and allowed pharmacies and individuals to import lower-priced drugs from Canada and other approved countries. It also required companies that patent drugs developed with federal research money to agree to reasonable prices first.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, roughly the entire senior and disabled population, would get a uniform government-run drug benefit with an 80% public share of drug costs, a hard $2,000 annual out-of-pocket cap, guaranteed coverage of any drug a doctor certifies as necessary, and a $25 monthly premium. The bill's findings note that the existing private-plan program left hundreds of thousands of low-income seniors unable to fill prescriptions in its first month and prohibited Medicare from negotiating prices, while Americans pay the highest brand-name drug prices in the world.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 2003 Medicare Part D structure and replaces it with a government-administered prescription benefit for all Medicare beneficiaries, run by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services rather than competing private plans.

Sets the public share at 80% of the negotiated price of each covered drug, with a catastrophic limit of $2,000 in annual out-of-pocket costs (rising in later years), and a $25 monthly premium for 2007.

Requires Medicare to establish negotiated price schedules with drug manufacturers, wholesalers, and pharmacies — a step the bill's findings say the 2003 law explicitly prohibited — and encourages automatic generic substitution.

Requires participating drug makers to sell covered drugs to pharmacies at the lowest of the lowest U.S. federal agency price, the Medicaid 'best price', or the lowest importable price, addressing what the findings call prices up to five times those paid in other countries.

Allows commercial and personal importation of qualifying prescription drugs from Canada, Australia, Japan, New Zealand, Switzerland, and the European Union through registered pharmacies and exporters, which the findings estimate could save consumers at least $38 billion a year.

Bars federal agencies from handing a patent on federally funded health research to a private company unless the company first agrees to reasonable pricing with the Secretary of Health and Human Services.

Includes special protections for low-income beneficiaries, with states able to enroll dually eligible people directly and federal payments for their premiums and cost-sharing, without requiring them to apply through Medicaid systems.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers would bear the largest cost, through negotiated prices capped at their lowest price anywhere, mandatory rebates when program spending exceeds a target growth rate, and loss of the protected Medicare market structure created in 2003. Private insurers and pharmacy benefit managers that run Part D plans would lose that business entirely, since Medicare would administer the benefit itself. The federal government would appropriate funds for the catastrophic benefit and government contributions, and taxpayers who fund federal research could no longer transfer patents to industry without reasonable-pricing agreements.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug makers and Part D insurers

drawbacks.text: Repealing the 2003 law as of December 31, 2006 and switching every beneficiary to a new program in one year would have been a major transition: seniors enrolled in private Part D plans, and employers receiving retiree-plan subsidies, would all have to move to the new system, and any rollout failure would fall on seniors, as the bill's own findings show happened when the 2003 program launched.

The $2,000 catastrophic cap and 20% coinsurance would have been less protective than some existing private plans' benefit designs, and Medicare Advantage enrollees would face a new cap on plan deductibles and coinsurance that could reduce the extra benefits some plans offered.

The bill's spending-growth target with automatic manufacturer rebates is a hard cost-control mechanism; the bill itself carves out 'breakthrough' and orphan drugs for seven years, an acknowledgment that blunt price pressure could reduce incentives to develop new medicines.
The Secretary's rebate and breakthrough-drug determinations would not be subject to administrative or judicial review, concentrating significant unilateral power in the executive branch.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Medicare beneficiaries the gains are large and concrete: lower prices through negotiation and importation, a simple uniform benefit, and a hard out-of-pocket cap. The serious costs fall almost entirely on pharmaceutical manufacturers and Part D insurers rather than on patients, though the one-year transition to a brand-new program carried real execution risk for seniors, and the price-pressure mechanism trades some incentive for new drug development against today's costs. On balance the bill was designed to shift billions from drug makers and insurers to seniors and taxpayers.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in February 2006, it was referred to two House committees and then to a Health subcommittee, and neither committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Rep. Bernie Sanders with 19 original cosponsors on February 1, 2006.
It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and additionally to the Ways and Means Committee on the day of introduction.
On February 17, 2006 it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health — its last recorded action.
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or further action is recorded before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers and the private insurers and pharmacy benefit managers running Medicare Part D were better off, because the program that routes Medicare's drug spending through private plans and bars direct price negotiation stayed in place. Seniors gained nothing from this bill's death, though they were spared a one-year transition to a new program.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers and Part D private insurers

for.name: Rep. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to replace the private-plan Medicare drug benefit with a government-run benefit with negotiated prices and importation.

for.name: 19 House cosponsors (18 Democrats, 1 Republican)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, including Reps. Kucinich, DeFazio, Lee, Conyers, McGovern, Kaptur, and Rep. Jo Ann Emerson, the sole Republican.

against.name: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Chair of the committee of primary referral (109th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup of the bill after it was referred; it went only to the Health subcommittee.

against.name: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Chair of the second committee of referral (109th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after its referral; no hearing or markup is recorded.

against.name: Pharmaceutical research and manufacturers
against.role: Industry facing negotiated prices, lowest-price mandates, and rebates
against.what_they_did: The 2003 Medicare law the bill sought to repeal had been shaped around industry priorities, including an explicit ban on Medicare negotiating drug prices; the industry vigorously opposed Medicare price negotiation during this era.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 cosponsors were Democrats except one, Rep. Jo Ann Emerson of Missouri; no Republican leadership action ever moved the bill, and the committee chairs who controlled its fate were Republicans.

industries.note: The bill forces manufacturers to sell to Medicare patients at their lowest price anywhere in the world, lets Medicare negotiate directly, imposes rebates when spending outpaces a target, and attaches reasonable-pricing conditions to federally funded research patents. Its gain from higher U.S. prices runs directly against the cost seniors pay at the pharmacy.

industries.industry: Private health insurers and pharmacy benefit managers running Medicare Part D
industries.note: Repealing Part D eliminates the private-plan structure these companies administer and profit from; the bill moves the benefit in-house at Medicare. Their interest in keeping the plan-based system ran against beneficiaries' interest in a simpler, cheaper benefit.

Pharmacies would charge the Medicare-negotiated price instead of setting their own margins, but the bill guarantees reasonable dispensing and consultation fees, requires access to any qualifying pharmacy, and offers bonus payments for rural pharmacists.

industries.industry: Canadian and foreign pharmacies and drug exporters
industries.note: Legalizing registered importation from Canada, Australia, Japan, New Zealand, Switzerland, and the EU creates a new customer base of American seniors seeking lower foreign prices; the savings run alongside consumers' interest.
